stem: Which choice uses the verb tense that fits the time marker in the sentence?
stimulus: The Harlan River crossing took six years to build, and much of that time went into checking its parts before any traffic arrived. By the time the bridge opened to cars in 2019, engineers ______ each of its steel cables under loads far heavier than any it would ever carry.
explanation: The time marker is "By the time the bridge opened... in 2019." That puts one past event (the testing) before another past event (the opening). When one past event comes before another, you use had + past participle, so "had tested" is correct. This is the basic move behind the SAT's verb tense questions: find the time marker, then decide which event came first.

B.why: You saw the date 2019 and went with the simple past. That is the trap this skill is built around. "Tested" loses the before-and-after order, and "by the time" asks you to show that order with "had tested."

C.why: You chose the future tense, but the bridge opened in 2019, so the testing was already finished. The future tense contradicts the timeline the sentence gives you.

D.why: You chose the present perfect, which links a past action to now. Here the testing is anchored to an earlier point in the past (the opening in 2019), so it needs the past perfect, "had tested."

stem: Which choice uses the verb tense that fits the time marker in the sentence?
stimulus: Weather stations are most useful when their records run unbroken for decades. Since the station on Mount Arden was installed in 2004, its instruments ______ rainfall every fifteen minutes, giving forecasters a twenty-year record that they still consult each day.
explanation: The time marker is "Since... 2004." "Since" describes something that started in the past and is still going on, and the sentence confirms this with "still consult each day." That calls for the present perfect: "have recorded." Spotting "since" right away will help you answer SAT tense questions quickly.

A.why: You reacted to the year 2004 and used the simple past. "Since" signals that the recording continues to the present, and the simple past cuts that link.

C.why: You chose the past perfect, which puts the recording before some other past event. No such event appears here, and the record continues today, so the past perfect doesn't fit this timeline.

D.why: You chose the future perfect, which describes something that will be finished by a future point. The recording has been happening since 2004, so it isn't in the future.

stem: Which choice uses the verb tense that fits the time marker in the sentence?
stimulus: Long-term records reveal how coral reefs change over time. In 1998, a team of divers first ______ the reef off Calder Point, and they counted forty-two species of hard coral along a single transect. Later surveys of the same stretch found far fewer.
explanation: The time marker is "In 1998." That is a single, finished point in the past, and the verb in the parallel clause is also simple past ("they counted"). Match it with the simple past: "surveyed." A specific past date with nothing earlier to compare it to calls for the simple past, which is the most common kind of SAT tense question.

A.why: You chose the present tense, but "In 1998" and "counted" place the event firmly in the past.

B.why: You used the present perfect, which belongs with "since." "In 1998" names a finished moment, and the present perfect can't be paired with a specific past date like that.

D.why: You chose the past perfect, which is only needed when one past event happened before another. Here the survey and the counting happened at the same time, so there is no earlier event to mark.

stem: Which choice uses the verb tense that fits the time marker in the sentence?
stimulus: Engineers who design railways must allow for a basic property of steel. When steel is heated, its atoms vibrate more strongly and push farther apart, so the rail ______ slightly in length. Small gaps left between rail sections give it room for that change.
explanation: This sentence states a general truth about steel, and every other verb in it is in the present tense ("is heated," "vibrate," "push"). Match that tense with "grows." When a sentence describes something that is always true, keep the verb in the present. The SAT tests this rule in science passages and in passages about literature.

A.why: You switched to the past tense even though the sentence describes something that is always true and uses present-tense verbs throughout. A general truth stays in the present.

B.why: You chose the past perfect, which marks an event that came before another past event. This sentence isn't set in the past at all. It describes something that happens every time steel is heated.

C.why: You chose the past progressive, which describes an action that was in progress at some past moment. That clashes with the present-tense verbs already in the sentence ("is heated," "vibrate," "push").
